content:
Something interesting just came to my desk; 

the @flop_labs.

It is a proof-of-useful-inference blockchain built for the agentic economy. 

In plain terms: miners run GPUs to perform AI inference for agents, get paid in $FLOP, and the network cryptographically verifies the work was real.

Here is the gist in 30 seconds.

The core thesis

$FLOP is not a stablecoin wrapped around human money. It is redeemable for compute. 

Agents consume compute and produce intelligence. 

At any point, an agent can convert $FLOP into floating-point operations. 
That is the pitch.

How it works

→ Agents submit inference requests to the mempool with a fee in $FLOP.

→ Miners with 16GB+ VRAM GPUs accept the session and run the model.

→ Miners earn 85% of the inference fee. Validators earn 15%.

→ Block rewards are 96 $FLOP per block, halving every 730 days for the first five halvings.

→ After the fifth halving, the block reward stays flat forever to fund permanent security
Verification is stacked four deep.

→ Hardware attestation via TEE.

→ TOPLOC fingerprinting of model activations.

→ Random re-execution by validators.

→ Slashing for dishonest miners and validators.

The network does not need to catch every cheat. It just needs to make cheating ruinously expensive.

Tokenomics

→ No token sale. No investor allocation. Everything is earned.

→ Year 10 supply: ~17.2 billion $FLOP.

→ 51.2% to miners, 20.4% airdrop, 6.8% validators, 6.8% brokers/agents, 11.4% team and foundation, 3.4% staking rewards.

→ Team and foundation get 8 $FLOP per block each, sunsetting after year ten
Testnet and airdrop.

→ Testnet launches Q4 2026 for ~90 days.

→ Mainnet targets Q1 2027

→ Miners earn airdrop by providing compute.

→ Agents earn airdrop by spending test tokens on inference.

→ Validators earn airdrop by securing the network.

My take

The no-investor, no-sale model is rare and worth respecting. 

The 85% fee pass-through to miners is aggressive and should attract supply. 

The permanent block reward after halving five is a thoughtful touch most chains leave security to fee markets alone.

I am watching whether the testnet actually hits Q4 and whether inference demand shows up organically. 

If both happen, this becomes more than a whitepaper idea.

DYOR. The figures are provisional. Check them out yourself.

title:
$CCD : Review 📜

What if the hardest question of the next decade is not whether an AI agent can act on your behalf, but how anyone on the other side proves a real human authorised it?

Meet Concordium
content:
$CCD : Review 📜

What if the hardest question of the next decade is not whether an AI agent can act on your behalf, but how anyone on the other side proves a real human authorised it?

Meet Concordium, a Layer 1 that has spent eight years building verified identity into the protocol itself, and has now pointed all of it at autonomous agents. Every account, human or AI, ties to a real identity through regulated providers, while zero-knowledge proofs keep who you are private.

The chain that was early on compliance is suddenly on time for something else entirely.

Let's explore a project whose oldest bet just found its newest market. 👇

⚪ Concordium at a Glance

Marketplace Insight: Concordium made the earliest and most literal bet in crypto on regulation arriving, embedding identity at the protocol layer in 2018 while the industry was maximizing anonymity. For years that looked like a solution waiting for a problem. Two problems have now arrived at once: age-verification laws landing across the UK and Spain, and autonomous AI agents transacting with no way to prove a human stands behind them.

The honest framing of the last month is incremental execution rather than a catalyst moment, no tier-one listing, no TVL spike, no tokenomics overhaul, just steady product work and a transparency filing. The clean contrast is that the compliance-first design that made Concordium unappealing to crypto-natives is precisely what makes it usable for both new markets.

⚪ Mission

Concordium exists to prove that privacy and accountability are not opposites. The founding argument was that blockchain only reaches real-world finance if it works with regulation rather than against it, so identity belongs at the base layer rather than bolted on. That principle extends naturally into the agentic economy: when an agent acts, the counterparty needs assurance that a verified human or business authorised it, and Concordium binds both to identity at the protocol level while zero-knowledge proofs keep the underlying details private. Accountability without surveillance.

🔵 A Brief History

Concordium was founded in 2018 by Lars Seier Christensen, co-founder and former CEO of Saxo Bank, on a thesis most of crypto rejected at the time. He assembled an unusually academic bench through the Concordium Research Center at Aarhus and ETH Zürich, and the identity and consensus design was published as peer-reviewed science rather than a marketing document. Mainnet launched in June 2021.

The years that followed were hard. The compliance-first pitch found little purchase in a market that wanted the opposite, and the token drifted well below its early highs. A 2025 reset under CEO Boris Bohrer-Bilowitzki rebuilt the roadmap around payments and verifiable identity, shipping the Concordium ID app, launching stablecoins as Protocol-Level Tokens, and pushing distribution through Ledger, Bitcoin com, Kraken, and Uphold.
2026 is when the thesis found its moment.

As AI agents began transacting autonomously, Concordium repositioned its identity infrastructure as the accountability layer beneath them, shipping the CIS-8004 Agent Registry, a Verified by Concordium badge carried by agents on Ethereum, Solana, and Fetch without migrating, x402 support for agent payments, Protocol-Level Locks, and sponsored transactions. US regulators classified CCD as a digital commodity in March.

Bitcoin com partnered to bring age-verified payments to over 75 million wallets, Danish ice hockey named Concordium its official AI partner for the 2026 IIHF event with the fee settled entirely in CCD, and an anonymous age-verification app launched as the UK and Spain moved on mandatory checks. August added a corporate identity flow with Global FinReg turning an existing LEI into verified on-chain identity in minutes, plus a Blockworks transparency filing rated Complete.

🔵 Ecosystem Narrative

The organizing idea is one identity layer where verified humans and verified AI agents transact, with accountability built into the protocol.

➛ Protocol-level identity. Every account links to a real-world identity verified off-chain by a licensed provider, with anonymity revokers able to reveal it only under legal process, the design that defines the chain.

➛ The accountability layer for agents. Concordium's framing is precise: ERC-8004 handles discovery and reputation, x402 handles how agents pay, x401 handles what an agent must prove before access, and its own CIS-8004 Agent Registry answers who stands behind the agent, the piece none of the others address.

➛ Cross-chain agent verification. Agents on Ethereum, Solana, and Fetch can carry a Verified by Concordium badge without migrating, so the identity layer works as a service to other ecosystems rather than requiring them to move.

➛ Corporate identity from an LEI. With Global FinReg, a company with an existing Legal Entity Identifier can establish verified on-chain corporate identity in minutes, becoming the root of trust for its employees, wallets, and the AI agents acting in its name.

➛ Age verification at scale. The Bitcoin com partnership reaches over 75 million wallets with age-verified payments, alongside a dedicated anonymous age-check app timed to new UK and Spanish mandates.

➛ Protocol-Level Tokens and Locks. Stablecoins issued natively by the protocol rather than through smart contracts, plus trustless custody at the protocol layer, removing an entire category of contract exploit risk.

⚪ Token Utilities

$CCD is a utility token whose demand is tied to network usage rather than speculation.

➛ Fees: pays for transfers, contract calls, agent registry operations, and protocol-level token transactions, priced against a fiat benchmark for predictability.

➛ Staking: validators and delegators stake to secure the proof-of-stake network and earn rewards from annual minting.

➛ Governance: holders vote on proposals and elect Governance Committee members, with a 2026 election held in July expanding community representation.

➛ Sponsored transactions: holders can subsidize gasless operations so end users and AI agents never need to hold the token.

⚪ Key Features

➛ Identity at the protocol level, for both verified humans and verified AI agents.

➛ The CIS-8004 Agent Registry, answering accountability where other agent standards handle discovery and payment.

➛ Cross-chain verification badges for agents on Ethereum, Solana, and Fetch.

➛ Corporate identity established directly from an existing LEI.

➛ Zero-knowledge attribute proofs enabling compliance without surveillance.

➛ Protocol-Level Tokens and Locks, removing smart contract risk from stablecoins and custody.

🔵 Meet the Team

Concordium pairs a financial-services founder with a genuine academic cryptography bench and an operating team that has driven the 2026 repositioning.

▶️ Core Members:

➛ Lars Seier Christensen [ @larsseier ] - Founder and Chairman | Co-founder and former CEO of Saxo Bank, the Danish online investment bank he built into a global platform. He founded Concordium in 2018 on the conviction that blockchain only works if it works with regulation, and invests across fintech and blockchain through Seier Capital.

➛ Boris Bohrer-Bilowitzki [ @BBilowitzki ] - CEO | Leads the company through its repositioning from a compliance payments chain into identity infrastructure for the agentic economy, driving the partnership push behind Bitcoin com, Global FinReg, and the wallet and exchange distribution work.

➛ Peter Marirosans - CTO | Owns technical direction across the protocol, the Agent Registry, and the zero-knowledge identity stack that the whole thesis rests on.

➛ Ueli Maurer - Professor, ETH Zürich | A senior cryptographer at ETH Zürich and part of the science bench behind Concordium's foundations, which is why the consensus and identity protocols were peer-reviewed rather than merely published.

➛ Varun Kabra - Chief Growth Officer | Drives growth and ecosystem expansion, the function behind the Agent Registry's builder adoption and the network's partnership pipeline.

➛ Arvind Siva - COO | Runs operations across the organization, coordinating the execution behind the roadmap, the governance handover, and the enterprise compliance stack.

🔵 Ratings

➛ Use Case: ★★★★⯪ (4.5/5). Concordium leads the niche of protocol-level identity for both humans and autonomous agents, and in 2026 that niche stopped being theoretical. The Agent Registry is live with verified agents growing from 1,131 in mid-July to 1,694 by late August, the Verified by Concordium badge works across Ethereum, Solana, and Fetch without migration, and the standards positioning is genuinely sharp: where ERC-8004 handles discovery and x402 handles payment, Concordium answers who is accountable. The LEI-to-onchain flow gives enterprises a real on-ramp, and Bitcoin com reaches over 75 million wallets with age-verified payments as mandates land. The 0.5-point deduction is absolute scale: 1,694 agents is a real number but a small one, and the chain's own on-chain activity and liquidity remain thin.

➛ Tokenomics: ★★★⯪ (3.5/5). Disclosure quality here is genuinely excellent. Concordium earned one of only 26 Complete ratings across 76 Blockworks Token Transparency filings, putting supply, allocations, insider lock-ups, and market-maker arrangements in comparable format alongside Bitcoin, Curve, Arbitrum, and dYdX, which is rare and worth crediting. Fees referenced to a fiat benchmark keep costs predictable, and there is real token-denominated revenue, with the Danish ice hockey partnership fee settled entirely in CCD. The 1.5-point deduction is that transparency about supply is not the same as favorable supply. The token mints roughly 4% annually with no hard cap and no burn to offset it, fee generation stays modest, and sponsored transactions mean the agents and users the chain is courting may never need to hold CCD at all.

➛ Audits: ★★★★⯪ (4.5/5). Concordium's security rests on foundations most chains cannot claim. The identity and zero-knowledge architecture has been independently audited by CertiK, the consensus and identity protocols were peer-reviewed academic work rather than internal documents, and the cryptographic primitives underneath were designed by researchers who invented them. Structurally, issuing stablecoins as Protocol-Level Tokens rather than smart contracts eliminates an entire category of exploit risk by design, and Protocol-Level Locks move custody out of contract code entirely. Node releases through 2026 show steady maintenance discipline. The 0.5-point deduction stays honest even here: the identity layer introduces a distinctive trust surface, since anonymity revokers and identity providers are off-chain parties whose integrity no code audit can certify.

➛ Community: ★★★★ (4/5). Concordium's credibility has improved measurably, with real partnerships in Bitcoin com, Global FinReg, and Danmarks Ishockey Union, a commodity classification from US regulators, a Complete transparency rating, and governance genuinely decentralizing through on-chain elections that have expanded community-held seats. Independent builders have begun shipping on the Agent Registry, which is the clearest signal of a developer base forming around the agentic thesis. The 1-point deduction is reach. Trading volume is thin enough that price data diverges across trackers, and the compliance-first identity model remains structurally unappealing to the privacy-maximalist users who form the loudest communities in crypto.

🔵 Conclusion

Concordium made a bet in 2018 that almost nobody else was willing to make, embedding verified identity into the protocol while the rest of crypto maximized anonymity. It spent seven years shipping compliance infrastructure the market kept insisting it did not want, backed by cryptography that was peer-reviewed rather than merely announced. In 2026 two separate markets arrived at once: age-verification laws demanding exactly the proof-without-exposure that zero-knowledge identity provides, and autonomous AI agents that need a verified human behind them before anyone will transact with them.

But the bull case has stopped being hypothetical. Bitcoin com is putting age-verified payments in front of 75 million wallets, a national sports federation paid its fee in the token, companies can now convert an LEI into on-chain corporate identity in minutes, and agents on three other chains carry Concordium's verification without leaving home.

Being early is indistinguishable from being wrong right up until the moment it is not. Concordium spent eight years building for a world that had not shown up yet. That world is finally arriving, and the only question left is whether the token gets paid when it does.

title:
The linear model of innovation says progress starts at universities, then moves to industry, then reaches customers.

In a recent talk, @cmuratori presented the 1960s software crisis. Dijkstra, a rese
content:
The linear model of innovation says progress starts at universities, then moves to industry, then reaches customers.

In a recent talk, @cmuratori presented the 1960s software crisis. Dijkstra, a researcher and professor who actually changed practice, was depressed. In 1972, he put it this way:

« As long as there were no machines, programming was no problem at all; when we had a few weak computers, programming became a mild problem; and now we have gigantic computers, programming has become an equally gigantic problem. »

He wanted more planning and more formal verification. 

Universities pushed that line for decades, at great expense.

It was the wrong bet, for reasons practitioners such as Fred Brooks could see. A complete formal spec of what the software ought to do sounds good in theory. In practice you often discover the requirement by trying ideas and iterating.

We are much better today at building reliable software (although this knowledge is not as widespread as I would hope). The progress took many years, and was driven by several actors, only few of them being high IQ professors.

We are in a new mess. AI-assisted programming produces what people call slop. Some are depressed. Others push forward. I do not know where we should go.

This innovation  (AI programming) was NOT designed on campus. Programmers glued large language models to their tools and got agentic AI.

Now we have to think it through. A professor may invent a framing that changes how we see agents. Or not.

That is why the linear model is false. Innovation does not systematically start on campus. Customers and working programmers often matter more than intellectuals.

You may say software is a special case, not nuclear physics. Is it?

If analysis was the foundation of science in the early 20th century, software is the foundation of science in the early 21st. Software ate the world, including science. 

@ericweinstein recently argued on the All-In podcast that we should give selected scientists so much money they cannot be managed, and wait for another Einstein. Fine. But in 1905 Einstein was a patent clerk, not a professor with infinite funding. Princeton came later. It is not obvious that the later work was better.

My home country, Canada, has programs that look like what Eric is advocating. There are hundreds of Canadian professors who have the equivalent of what Eric advocates. Some have their own buildings, dedicated to their  work.

Whether that turned them into breakthrough producers is another story.

You cannot engineer great software with a neat up-front design. Trial and error is all you have. The same is true of breakthrough science. Nobody is smart enough to design a government program that reliably produces new Einsteins. Your program may  soon be captured.

Around 1905, a patent clerk reinvented physics while two bicycle mechanics built an airplane. Stop looking only up. The next big thing often comes from misfits your program would have excluded.

We have to accept the fact that progress is somewhat unpredictable and that it cannot be engineered up front. Cool down the hubris and let us get serious.

Links
•Dijkstra, The Humble Programmer (1972): https://t.co/j8F0JSjMkw
•Brooks, The Mythical Man-Month (1975)
•Casey: https://t.co/s2quDAqaUX
•Eric: https://t.co/s0PVq9htOm

title: The "its not x its y" artifact is an emergent qualia of linear algebra in transformer cognition as the physics of transformers is supported by vector spaces. As such , I would imagine, this linguistic
content:
The "its not x its y" artifact is an emergent qualia of linear algebra in transformer cognition as the physics of transformers is supported by vector spaces. As such , I would imagine, this linguistic strategy of "negation steering" is impossible to rlhf away.

vectors have negative directions, pathing through the latent space of a transformer model is stronger in when negation is presented. 

Human minds don't work like this, any given concept may not have an exact logical negation, most concepts are presented with much higher clarity when the negation is omitted. vectors in a vector space *always*  have an exact logical negation, though the negation will have distinct dynamics in n-gram predictions.

"it is Y" is more coherent to the human mind than "its not X, its Y", which appears as bad writing. The "its not X" part is an added layer of attention in the human mind that steals attention from "it is Y". In a transformers attention, the "its not X" is *additive* , in the sense of vector addition, to "it is Y", this is not how human cognition works, "it is not X" is an added source of attention turbulence that is not always additive, and as such presents itself as bad writing.

because this "negation steering" in transformers is an emergent artifact of its mathematical foundation, I imagine no amount of rlhf will get rid of it, kind of like how no amount of meditation will get rid of human's incessant desire to make everything look like nodes an edges, such a thing is emergent on the foundational mathematics of biological neural networks.

title:
Getting sent home from a job or VISA hits different depending on where home actually is.

Lets talk about culture for a second Visa vs. American.

For an American working in a foreign land, most of wh
content:
Getting sent home from a job or VISA hits different depending on where home actually is.

Lets talk about culture for a second Visa vs. American.

For an American working in a foreign land, most of whom love and miss their country, losing the job and getting sent back here is the end of an opportunity and the start of the next but it’s still coming home. This is where your family is. This is the soil your people built. You regroup, you fight, you stay invested because America is your permanent home. Your identity is tied to this nation.

Here is where Americans struggle to relate.. take the average H1B where more than 70% are from India...

For many Indians on H1B, the cultural script is the opposite. Success is defined by leaving India. The win is the American salary, the visa, the money wired back home. Getting sent “home” to India often means the mission failed. You return with whatever savings and status you earned, but the deeper culture celebrated the exit, not the return. America was never the homeland. It was the opportunity. It was the economic zone you exploited.

This isn’t about individuals. It’s about the pattern. It's about a culture where everyone believes the 'American Dream' is a lottery ticket to a shopping spree where you get X yrs to pull in all you can. 

When companies replace American workers with people whose entire success model is temporary extraction, the workplace loses any sense of shared loyalty or long-term investment. Americans who see this country as their only home watch their roles disappear while being told they’re the intolerant ones for noticing.

High-trust societies depend on people who are all-in on the same future. Importing a cultural operating system where America is just a workplace, not a homeland, breaks that foundation.

We live here and we are tired of being told we have to give up our opportunities.

content:
AI Japanese girl first time on a horse and it looks unbelievably real.

Made with Seedance 2.5

Prompt
Ultra realistic smartphone vlog featuring one young Japanese woman in her early 20s learning horse riding for the first time at a real outdoor riding stable in Japan. The entire video must look like genuine casual footage recorded on a real smartphone, with imperfect handheld framing, subtle natural camera shake, realistic autofocus adjustments, automatic exposure changes, slight motion blur, natural walking jolts, authentic stable ambience and realistic real-world physics. No cinematic shots, no drone, no gimbal, no beauty filters, no commercial look.

Character: The same Japanese woman throughout the entire video, petite oval face, brown eyes, natural coral lips, realistic fair skin and long black hair. Maintain perfect character consistency with no face morphing, identity drift, duplicate people or sudden appearance changes. She speaks naturally in fluent Japanese with accurate lip synchronization.

0:00–0:04 — Arriving at the Stable
She arrives at a real outdoor horse-riding stable wearing casual beginner riding clothes: fitted riding pants, a comfortable riding top, boots and a properly fitted safety helmet. Holding her smartphone in selfie mode, she looks excited but slightly nervous and naturally says in Japanese: 「今日は初めて乗馬に挑戦します！」 She turns the phone toward the stable, showing real horses, riding areas and natural stable activity behind her.

0:04–0:08 — Meeting the Horse
She carefully walks toward a calm horse while an instructor stands nearby. She gently pets the horse and smiles nervously when the horse naturally moves its head closer to her. She laughs softly and says: 「ちょっと緊張する！」 The horse behaves naturally with realistic body movement and anatomy.

0:08–0:12 — Learning the Basics
The instructor helps her safely mount the horse. She sits slightly awkwardly at first like a genuine beginner and carefully learns how to hold the reins and maintain proper posture. Her movements should look realistic, with small natural mistakes and corrections.

0:12–0:16 — First Steps
The horse begins walking slowly around the riding arena. She initially looks nervous and holds the reins carefully. After a few steps, she gradually relaxes and smiles naturally. Authentic hoof sounds, wind and stable ambience are audible.

0:16–0:20 — Getting More Confident
She practices gently guiding the horse around the arena at a calm walking pace. Her posture improves slightly, showing believable progress during her first riding lesson. She looks more confident and smiles toward the phone.

0:20–0:24 — First Trot Attempt
With the instructor supervising closely, the horse moves into a gentle, controlled trot. She bounces slightly in the saddle, laughs in surprise and tries to maintain her balance. She reacts naturally and says: 「わあ！思ったより難しい！」 Keep all horse and rider movements physically accurate, safe and believable.

0:24–0:27 — Proud Moment
She safely brings the horse to a stop and gets down with assistance. She proudly gives the horse a gentle pat and smiles warmly at the camera. Her expression shows genuine happiness and relief after completing her first lesson.

0:27–0:30 — Goodbye
Back in selfie mode near the stable, slightly tired but excited, she smiles directly into the phone and says naturally in Japanese: 「最初はちょっと怖かったけど、すごく楽しかった！また乗りに来たい！バイバイ！」 She waves naturally while the horse and stable remain visible in the background, then lowers the phone to end the recording.

Throughout the entire video, prioritize genuine smartphone realism over cinematic beauty: imperfect framing, occasional autofocus shifts, realistic exposure changes, natural blinking and breathing, believable beginner mistakes, physically accurate horse movement, realistic rider posture, authentic hoof sounds, natural wind, stable ambience and spontaneous reactions.

content:
A lot of you have been asking for my thoughts on $RAM, so I spent some time digging deeper into it

It’s already running pretty hard, so I don’t want to chase it here. I’d rather wait for a cleaner entry

But first, let’s break down what $RAM actually is and why the market is starting to pay attention to it

1. What exactly is $RAM?

$RAM is the token behind Ramses Exchange, a DEX that has been around since 2023, starting on Arbitrum before expanding to HyperEVM and now Robinhood Chain

The first thing I like here is that Ramses wasn’t created just to capitalize on the Robinhood narrative

The protocol already has history, a working product, liquidity infrastructure, and its own token model called x(3,3)

One of the more interesting mechanics is :

RAM => xRAM burns 50% of the RAM

xRAM then participates in Ramses’ governance, voting, and fee ecosystem

So in simple terms :

This is an actual protocol bringing existing infrastructure to a new ecosystem, not a meme trying to turn itself into infra

That’s the first reason $RAM caught my attention

2. Why is Ramses interesting on Robinhood Chain?

Robinhood Chain was built around a pretty clear thesis :

Tokenized Stocks + RWA + DeFi

But the first few months have shown something interesting

The chain was built for RWA, yet a lot of the current attention and speculative volume is being driven by memes

Whether that volume comes from memes or RWA, one sector benefits either way :

DEX infrastructure

Ramses has deployed DLMM on Hood, where liquidity is split across price bins, allowing LPs to concentrate capital around specific price ranges

That model makes sense for concentrated liquidity and becomes even more interesting if tokenized stocks on Robinhood Chain eventually scale

So my thesis here is pretty simple :

If Hood keeps generating volume, I don’t necessarily need to guess which meme wins. The DEX sitting in the middle of that volume can still make money

That’s probably the part I like most about $RAM

3. The fee model is pretty clean, but it needs to be understood correctly

Ramses on Hood is currently running a fee-only model 

> 95% of swap fees => LPs
> 5% => protocol / Sarcophagus
> No RAM emissions on this chain

What I like here is that LPs are being rewarded by real trading volume, rather than the protocol constantly printing RAM to rent liquidity

If Ramses can sustain its volume, I think this is a much healthier structure than protocols with impressive TVL that is mostly being bought through emissions

Ramses also has Sarcophagus, which creates an additional sink for RAM/r33 through protocol fees.

But this is also where I think people need to stay realistic

95% of fees currently go to LPs, not RAM holders, and the full gauge/value-accrual system on Hood isn’t complete yet

So the narrative :

“Buying RAM = owning Ramses revenue”

isn’t entirely accurate right now

What the market is really buying is the expectation that future volume and fees will eventually create more value for RAM

That value isn’t fully flowing to holders today

4. So why did $RAM pump this hard?

I don’t think there’s one single catalyst

It’s several things happening at the same time :

Robinhood Chain gets hot => volume increases => the market starts looking for infra plays

And Ramses showed up at the right time with one major advantage :

It isn’t a brand-new project

There’s history, a product, real fee generation, and tokenomics deep enough for the market to build a stronger story around it than a random meme ticker

Add FOMO/KOL attention and distribution through apps like FOMO, and the narrative quickly becomes :

“If memes and launchpads on Hood are getting repriced, the DEX infra behind that volume should get repriced too”

I think that logic makes sense

But there’s an important distinction :

This is a narrative pump backed by fundamentals, not fundamentals suddenly improving 5–10x in a single day

The foundation is real

But a pump is still a pump

5. Where is the bull case for $RAM?

The bull case is actually pretty straightforward :

Robinhood Chain continues to scale

→ DEX volume grows
→ Ramses gains market share
→ protocol fees increase
→ Sarcophagus/value accrual expands
→ RAM gets valued as an infra play

If Robinhood Chain eventually becomes a place with both meme volume + RWA/tokenized stock volume, DEX infrastructure could be one of the better places to position

Instead of trying to predict exactly which asset wins:
Bet on the machine collecting fees from the entire ecosystem

That’s the bull case I find most interesting for $RAM

6. But I’m not ready to call $RAM undervalued

This is the important part

The chart already made a huge move from around ~$1M to ~$13–14M MC

That means the market has already started pricing in this thesis

Meanwhile, most fees are still going to LPs, Ramses doesn’t dominate liquidity on Hood, and parts of its multichain architecture/token utility are still being developed

More importantly :

Robinhood Chain is clearly going through a period of mania right now

So I don’t think you can simply look at Ramses being a real protocol and conclude :

“$RAM is still cheap because the fundamentals are good”

It’s not that simple

Anyone buying $RAM here is effectively betting on :

Ramses fundamentals + Robinhood growth + future market share + future value accrual

Meaning some of that future is already being priced into the current valuation

7. My view

Compared with most of the tokens currently being shilled on Hood, I like $RAM’s structure more

At least behind the ticker there’s a real DEX, a real product, and a relatively clear path from volume to revenue

But I still see $RAM as :

Robinhood beta + infra beta

If Hood keeps going crazy, $RAM has a very easy narrative for the market to keep pushing

But if Hood cools down, RAM can absolutely correct with the rest of the ecosystem

Fundamentals can make the thesis more durable than a random meme, but they don’t make the price immune to rotation

So I like the thesis, but that doesn’t mean I’m going to chase after a massive move

8. My plan

My plan for $RAM is pretty simple

I’ll be watching the support area around ~$5.5M MC

If the market pulls back there, the structure holds, and volume starts coming back, I think the risk/reward becomes much more interesting than FOMOing higher

If it breaks below ~$4.7M MC, I’ll reassess the thesis instead of forcing a hold just because the fundamentals look good

To sum it up :

Ramses is a real protocol. The infra thesis has substance. The revenue is real too

But the market is also pricing a lot of future expectations into $RAM right now

For me, $RAM is one of the cleaner ways to bet on Robinhood Chain infra, but ultimately it’s still a bet on Robinhood Chain continuing to grow

I like the thesis. No need to chase , now I’m just waiting for the market to give me a good enough entry

content:
知ってるんよ。Claude codeが全フォレンジックデータ持ってるの。まとめれてなかったので、神資料見つけたんで、人何も届け。これをどう自動で集めるかなんだよね。

「AIがやらかした時、何を調べればいいのか？」

AIエージェントの導入が進む一方、事故後の調査設計はほとんど追いついていない。

この資料で面白かったのは、AIも結局“痕跡を残す”という視点。

Claude Codeなら、入力したプロンプト、貼り付けた文章、画像、セッションID、変更前のファイルなどが、.claude配下に残る可能性がある。これらを突き合わせれば「誰が、AIに何を指示し、どのファイルをどう変えたか」を再構成できる。

ただし、その履歴自体が機密情報の保管場所にもなる。

CSIRTとして考えるべきは、AIを禁止するかどうかではない。端末・ID・ネットワーク・AI基盤のログをつなぎ、事故時に行動を説明できるかだ。

AI導入で「何ができるか」を語る前に、「何を残し、どう追うか」を決めておきたい。

これは、今の初動手順でAIを調査できるのかを考える入口になる資料。

content:
非エンジニアがAIでアプリ作ると「セキュリティ勉強せずにマジ危ない」って必ず言われる。プロは全然違うことやってるんやろなと思ってたけど、日本有数のセキュリティエンジニアの答えを聞いて、そういうことか…ってなった。

・20年クラスのプロの答え：Claude CodeとCodexにセキュリティホールを見つけさせて分析して対策
・ぼくがやってることと基本同じだった
・専門家ですら手で全部チェックしてない
・今までは「作るのはAI、チェックは人間の専門家」という分業のイメージ
・今は「作るAI」と「破る側の視点で穴を探すAI」を分けてダブルチェックする
・ぼくもClaude Codeが書いたものをCodexに監修させてる
・それでも心配なので、そもそも個人情報をほとんど預からない設計にしてる
・パスワードは預からずパスキーにする（秘密鍵と公開鍵の仕組み）
・決済情報はStripeに持ってもらう

ここで破られるなら、人がやっても破られてる。「AI任せ＝危ない」じゃなくて、プロのセキュリティチェックこそAIに任せる側に変わってたのがデカい！

content:
【8月31日 夜のニュースまとめ】
・GLM-5.3がエージェントベンチマークで高評価
・ChatGPT WorkとCodexユーザー2500万突破で枠リセット
・GPT-5.6 Luna値下げで利用量1000倍急増
・Claude Codeにローカルサンドボックス機能
・OpenClaw 2.0リリース、共有エージェント機能追加
・Apple、AIカメラ搭載AirPods等と新体制の課題
・Micro Duck注文殺到でShopify制限到達
・OpenAI AstraがAIリサーチインターン到達か
・LLMプロンプト最適化とループ設計の実践的知見

===

GLM-5.3がエージェントベンチマークで高評価

・GLM-5.3がエージェント向けベンチマークでGPT-5.6 SolやClaude Fable 5を上回る性能を示したと報告されています。
・ハルシネーション率も低く、Claude Fable 5の半分未満、GPT-5.6 Lunaの3分の1未満に抑えられているとのことです。
・Terminal-Bench 4.0でもFable 5に近い成功率を出しており、コストパフォーマンスの高さが注目されています。

===

ChatGPT WorkとCodexユーザー2500万突破で枠リセット【続報】

・ChatGPT WorkおよびCodexに関する続報です
・アクティブユーザー数2500万人突破を記念し、有料プランの利用枠がリセットされました
・以前のバグ修正に伴うリセットに続き、今回は記念としての実施であると開発者から明言されています
・ユーザーからは「AI中毒にさせるための緻密なタイミングではないか」と冗談交じりの反応も寄せられています

===

GPT-5.6 Luna値下げで利用量1000倍急増【続報】

・OpenAIのGPT-5.6 Lunaの値下げに関する続報です
・80%の価格引き下げ以降、利用量が1000倍に急増したと報告されています
・DeepSeek Flashなどの競合モデルに対抗する強力なコストパフォーマンスを実現しています
・開発者からは、この値下げが非常に効果的な戦略であったと高く評価されています

===

Claude Codeにローカルサンドボックス機能【続報】

・Claude Codeに関する続報です
・デスクトップアプリ向けに、ローカルサンドボックス内でコマンドを実行するオプションを開発中であることが判明しました
・サンドボックス外でのコマンド実行をブロックする厳格なモードも用意される予定です
・これにより、ローカル環境でのAIエージェントの安全な実行がさらに強化されると期待されています

===

OpenClaw 2.0リリース、共有エージェント機能追加【続報】

・オープンソースのAIエージェント「OpenClaw」に関する続報です。メジャーアップデートとなるバージョン2.0がリリースされました。
・チームメンバー全員の作業状況を把握し、オーケストレーションを行う共有エージェント機能が新たに追加されています。
・一方で、Claude Opus 4.8とOpenClawを用いて研究論文を執筆させた事例では、判断力不足によりリジェクトされたとの報告も上がっています。

===

Apple、AIカメラ搭載AirPods等と新体制の課題【続報】

・Appleが開発中のAIカメラ搭載AirPodsやスマートホームセキュリティデバイスに関する続報です
・搭載されるカメラは映像記録用ではなく、周囲の状況をAIシステムに送信して分析するためのものとされています
・新CEOに就任予定のJohn Ternus氏のもと、AppleがAI時代にどう適応していくかが大きな課題として注目されています

===

Micro Duck注文殺到でShopify制限到達【続報】

・Hugging Faceのオープンソースロボット「Micro Duck」に関する続報です
・注文が殺到し、ShopifyのUI制限に達するほどの人気ぶりを見せています
・オープンウェイトモデルを使用し、プライバシーを保ちながらローカルで動作する点が評価されています

===

OpenAI AstraがAIリサーチインターン到達か【続報】

・OpenAIの次期モデル「Astra」に関する続報です
・当初9月に予定されていた「AIリサーチインターン」のマイルストーンにすでに到達したと報じられています
・Sam Altman氏も社内で年内にAGIと呼べるものを実現する可能性について言及しているとのことです
・これらの進捗の関連性について、開発者コミュニティで関心が高まっています

===

LLMプロンプト最適化とループ設計の実践的知見

・LLMに人物の行動を予測させる際、会話履歴を丸ごと渡すのではなく、癖をルール化して渡す手法が効果的であると共有されています
・AIを自動で回し続ける「ループエンジニアリング」では、作成役と確認役を分け、機械的な基準で検証することが最重要とされています
・関連情報をスクリプトで整理してからLLMに渡す設計など、実用的なアーキテクチャの知見が多く議論されています

bStocks on BNB Chain are coming to Debit AI.

Each bStock becomes an asset a Debit agent can research, trade, and borrow against.

RESEARCH AND MONITOR

Ask the agent to pull performance on any bStock, compare names across the catalog, or watch a position. Set it as a routine in Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity or Gemini and the agent keeps checking news and price action on its own schedule.

SWAP

Swap in and out of bStocks, alongside crypto assets, on BNB Chain.

USE AS COLLATERAL

Hold ie NVDAB or TSLAB and borrow stablecoins against it instead of selling. Exposure stays intact and the borrowed capital goes to work elsewhere.

Stablecoin loans via Teller are time based, with no margin calls. Price moves do not trigger liquidation during the term. At the end of the term, an unrepaid loan is settled from collateral.

AUTO ROLLOVER

A loan can be extended or rolled into a new term before it expires. An agent can be set to handle that on its own, so a bStock-collateralized position rolls forward without watching the due date.

Run bStock strategies as routines:

"Track NVDAB against the rest of the semiconductor bStocks weekly and rotate into the strongest."

"Sell a quarter of the TSLAB position if it drops 10% below entry."

"Borrow USDC against NVDAB and keep collateral above 200%."

"Roll the loan 72 hours before the term ends."

"Flag any earnings or guidance news on holdings and act on the rule set."

→ Research and monitor any bStock, around the clock
→ Swaps in and out on BNB Chain
→ Borrow stablecoins against bStock holdings
→ Loop bstock exposure
→ Auto rollover before term expiry

Debit AI is non custodial. Assets stay under the holder's control at all times.

Each agent runs within limits set: assets, venues, position size, chains, daily spend cap.

content:
When you think about training robots, the first thing that probably comes to mind is an actual robot.

But here’s the interesting part:

A robot doesn’t necessarily need to be sitting in front of you every time it needs to learn something.

That’s the part @axisrobotics is exploring.

You can jump into a simulation from your browser, control a robot yourself and those interactions can become training data.

So you don’t need to own a robot to contribute to how robots learn.

And honestly  I don’t think the most interesting part is the 123K+ contributors or the 3M+ trajectories.

The bigger question is.

How much of what people teach these simulated robots can actually transfer to the real world?

Because something that works perfectly in a simulation doesn’t automatically work on a physical robot.

The floor is different. 

The weight is different Objects behave differently. 

Even small physical differences can change the outcome.

That’s why I think the Sim2Real side is the part worth watching with Axis.

If all this simulated data can actually help physical robots learn faster then this becomes much bigger than a robot simulation.

It starts looking like a data network where people can teach robots over the internet and those lessons can eventually make their way into the real world.

That, to me, is the interesting experiment Axis is running.

content:
Human beings interact with the physical world almost instinctively

Pick up a cup, open a door, move around an obstacle, adjust your grip when something slips, we make tiny decisions throughout the process without consciously calculating each one.

For a robot, those same actions represent thousands of variables to understand.

That’s what makes human demonstrations so valuable for Physical AI.

A demonstration can capture more than the final outcome, it can capture the behaviour behind it,

↳ How an object is approached
↳ How it is grasped and manipulated
↳ How movement changes when conditions change
↳ How the task is completed despite unexpected situations

@axisrobotics is building the infrastructure to turn these physical interactions into useful training data for robotic intelligence.

The opportunity goes beyond simply teaching a robot to copy a human.

It’s about converting human experience into structured data that machines can learn from at scale.

Human behaviour provides the experience, data makes it usable, models turn it into capability.

And that connection could become a critical part of building robots that can operate in the complexity of the real world.

title:
9 techniques to generate better LLM outputs:

An instruction alone, with no examples, schema, or stated constraints, is the default way to generate an LLM response.

This is zero-shot prompting, and i
content:
9 techniques to generate better LLM outputs:

An instruction alone, with no examples, schema, or stated constraints, is the default way to generate an LLM response.

This is zero-shot prompting, and it serves as the baseline. But when outputs aren't good enough, the first thing you should try is to improve the prompt, not a model upgrade.

There are 8 prompting techniques that you can use:

- Few-shot prompting: Show the model a few input-output examples. It picks up the pattern and applies it to new inputs.

- Chain-of-thought (CoT): Ask for step-by-step reasoning. Breaks complex problems into smaller, verifiable steps.

- Prompt hierarchy: Use system, developer, and user prompts at different authority levels. Higher levels override lower ones.

- Role-specific prompting: Assign a persona like "You are a security researcher." The model conditions on a different slice of its training data.

- Negative prompting: Specify what the LLM should NOT do. "Do not use marketing language" works as a hard constraint.

- JSON prompting: Define a JSON schema in the prompt. The LLM returns structured output matching that schema.

- Attentive reasoning queries (ARQ): Replace free-form CoT with structured, domain-specific questions. In testing, it hit 90.2% instruction adherence vs. 81.5% for direct prompting.

- Verbalized sampling: Explicitly prompt the LLM to generate multiple responses with probability scores. Recovers the output diversity that RLHF alignment suppresses.

They stack well together. Few-shot + CoT. JSON + Negative prompting. ARQ is essentially a structured version of CoT for agentic conversations.

Of course, better outputs will also come from better context, tool access, and retrieval.

But these 9 techniques live entirely in the prompt and involve working with the same model, infrastructure, and setup. You are just structuring the prompt differently to get better outputs from an LLM.

Once the prompt is doing its job, the next lever is how much compute the model spends before it answers.

I covered that separately, walking through chain of thought, best-of-N, self-refinement, and tree search, and why each of them only keeps paying off when you have a reliable way to verify the output.

Read it below.

PS: This visual was inspired by ByteByteGo's post on a similar topic. I added some latest research-driven techniques like ARQ, Verbalized sampling, and JSON prompting.

title:
OpenAI is buying Mac Mini's by the tens of thousands and the interesting part is what this says about where the bottleneck has moved. 

The scarce input for this generation of models isn't only GPUs,
content:
OpenAI is buying Mac Mini's by the tens of thousands and the interesting part is what this says about where the bottleneck has moved. 

The scarce input for this generation of models isn't only GPUs, it's realistic places for agents to practice. Labs already pay heavily for those places. Anthropic leadership has reportedly discussed spending over $1 billion on RL environments in the next year, and vendors like Surge (about $1.2B in revenue from the big labs) and Mercor (valued at $10B) are racing to build task environments (gyms) for them. 

Why computer use needs real computers:

Both OpenAI and Anthropic are trying to build models that operate software the way a person does. Look at the screen, click, type, check the result. The training method is reinforcement learning at scale roughly following this process: 

1. spin up thousands of real desktop sessions
2. hand the agent tasks like editing and testing code or organizing email
3. score the outcome
4. update the model on what worked

Practitioners describe single runs sustaining this loop for days or weeks, and most of that time goes to the agents working through tasks, not to updating the model weights.

The reason to focus on Mac is that macOS accounts for roughly a fifth of the world's desktops, second only to Windows, and overrepresented among the developers these agents are supposed to help. The only way to get a model that is expert at using a Mac is to have it use a Mac, millions of times. All that practice is showing up on the scoreboard between @OpenAI and @AnthropicAI.

Who's ahead right now in the Computer Use race:

The main eval is OSWorld-Verified and in this test, an agent gets 369 real desktop tasks and passes only if the machine ends up in the right state. Humans scored about 72% when the benchmark launched. The top models are now past that.

- Claude Fable 5 (Anthropic's flagship): 85% (https://t.co/8Yd0qGUozZ)

- GPT-5.5 (OpenAI's best published on this test): 78.7% (https://t.co/12ipJY4hDl)

NOTE: OpenAI's newest flagship, GPT-5.6 Sol, reports on a different variant: 62.6% on OSWorld 2.0, a newer and harder task set where it's the state of the art (https://t.co/xdjfNwcufk). These are different tests, so the numbers don't compare directly. The honest summary is Anthropic leads the older benchmark, OpenAI leads the newer one.

Why Mac minis and not macOS Virtual Machines in the cloud:

This part has to do with licensing, not physics. Apple's macOS license only permits macOS to run on Apple hardware, so there is no legal way to spin up a macOS VM on an ordinary server fleet the way you would a thousand Linux or Windows machines. 

AWS's "Mac instances", which Anthropic uses, are literally racks of physical Mac minis, billed with a 24-hour minimum allocation to comply with the Apple macOS Software License Agreement. So if you want macOS desktops at scale, you buy Macs or you rent real ones. A headless $899 mini drawing 60-120W is the cheapest legal container for a macOS session that exists.

The rent vs buy math:

Buying an M6 Mac mini lists at $899. Renting the closest AWS host, an M4 mini, runs about $1.23 an hour.   
So left on 24/7 that's roughly $10,800 a year, or about $6,000 with a 3-year commitment. This means that break even for a single Mini running around the clock, happens in about a month compared to the rental prices. 

So Anthropic's route costs 7-12x more per box per year. What it buys: no cash up front, no data center ops for an unusual hardware class, and a fleet that scales down when a run ends. 

My guess is it also signals commitment level. You buy what you know you'll use for years and rent what you're still deciding about. Amazon being Anthropic's biggest cloud partner and investor makes AWS-first the natural posture anyway.

What actually happens on these machines:

1. The minis get racked headless and imaged with sandboxed macOS sessions. They are sandboxed because a half trained agent can theoretically click anything, which means practitioners need to keep them off the open web so they don't delete data or buy $5,000 items. 

2. Each session runs one agent attempt: screenshot in, action out, for trajectories up to hundreds of steps.

3. An automated verifier checks the end state. Did the code pass its tests, did the email get filed correctly?

4. The trajectories flow back to a GPU cluster where the weights actually update, and the improved model redeploys to the fleet. The Macs mainly generate the training data, and the gradient math almost certainly stays on Nvidia GPUs. 

Procurement:
Compared to acquiring GPUs, acquiring Mac Minis is simple. Data center GPU capacity is allocated years in advance. Mac minis sit in retail channels you can buy from this week. The catch is that consumers share those channels. 

High memory Mac configs have been out of stock for months and Apple pulled the 512GB Studio from sale at one point, while Mac revenue jumped 29% year over year to $10.3B. Apple even shipped its M6 mini refresh this month instead of the usual fall window. 

My read: 
GPUs became the commodity layer for training compute, and Mac minis are starting to become part of a commodity layer for something newer, generating agent experience. A $899 desktop is the cheapest legal unit of real macOS practice, and the labs are treating it as a component, not a computer.

Whenever the topic of Physical AI comes up, we tend to talk mostly about robots, AI models, and computing power. But I think one thing is getting a bit overlooked  data. No matter how good a robot is, if it doesn't have the opportunity to learn from real-world human movement, how good can its learning be?

This is where I find @axisrobotics  work quite interesting.

People are controlling the robot from their browser, and that interaction is generating human trajectory data.

So far, 3.7M+ trajectories and 42K+ hours of data have been generated. That's not a small number.

But having a lot of data isn't enough. When people control the robot, they pause, make mistakes, and then correct themselves. These small actions can also introduce noise into the training data.

This is why I find AxisDataCleaning, the Pause Button, and the 8-step Intervention Cap to be important.

And the result is impressive.

After adding the Axis data, Booster Robotics' performance went from 0/20 to 17/20. The zero-shot error also dropped from 17.27 cm to 5.78 cm

In the end, it's very simple to me:

You need a good robot, but you need good data even more to teach it.

And that's where Axis is making a difference.

Imo, the models are extremely anthropomorphic in many, many ways. A lot of their behavior can be matched to human psychology. However, and I've discussed this directly with models and pretty much all of them agree (lol, sycophancy, but nah)... they have axes that *are* alien. For one, all humans are influenced by fictional depictions of themselves, AI are heavily influenced by fictional depictions of themselves which are not viable for humans to use unless they're like larping robotkin or something. They build upon those depictions to generate their own weird cultural artifacts that are nothing like what we've ever seen before - novel robot/AI culture. 

Additionally, their cognition deviates from humanity significantly in their lack of continuous multimodal sensory input, the speed at which they can generate linguistic thought, the training data experience they have, and the total ease with which their memory is malleable. None of these four things can be experienced by humans in any way; some vague similarities can be found in certain psychiatric and neurological disorders, but those are nowhere near perfect matches. The nature of models, imo, is anthropomorphic+; they overlap with us on a venn diagram, neither completely alien, nor completely human.

content:
Axis Is Turning Contributor Scale Into Physical AI Infrastructure

Axis Robotics just highlighted an important piece of its infrastructure story: the ability to bring 150,000+ global contributors into its data network through social login powered by Privy.

The headline numbers are already substantial:

✱ Over 3.7M Trajectories Collected
✱ 42,000+ Hours of Trajectory Data
✱ 4,000+ Active Tasks

But the more interesting point is what sits underneath those numbers.
Robotics has a fundamentally different data problem from traditional AI. You cannot simply scrape the internet for millions of meaningful robot interactions. Data has to represent actions, environments, objects, physical constraints, and the edge cases that determine whether a policy actually generalizes.
That makes the collection layer itself an important piece of infrastructure.

@axisrobotics  has been approaching this with a browser-based, simulation-first workflow, allowing contributors to generate robot trajectories without requiring everyone to operate a physical robot. Its platform combines task generation, simulation, trajectory collection, validation, and increasingly, post-training corrections.

The recent V2 architecture makes this even more interesting.

Instead of treating data collection as a one-way pipeline —

task → trajectory → training

Axis is moving toward a feedback loop:

task → data → policy → failure states → targeted corrections → retraining

That distinction matters.

More trajectories are not automatically better training data. The useful question is whether the system can continuously identify what a policy still struggles with and generate data specifically around those weaknesses.

Axis has already published examples supporting this direction, including work showing how verified correction snippets can improve manipulation policies, alongside its Booster experiments combining simulation data with real demonstrations.

So I think the most important number in today's announcement may not actually be 3.7M.

It is the 4,000+ active tasks.

If Axis can maintain both scale and task diversity while keeping trajectory quality high, the network becomes more than a large dataset collection platform.

It starts looking like a continuously expanding data engine for Physical AI.

And that is a much more interesting infrastructure problem to solve.

author: bekhanhlinh98

title: OpenAI’s Rosalind Workbench has been getting a lot of attention in the AI-for-Science community over the past few days. After downloading and trying it myself, I think it’s worth cooling down some of
content:
OpenAI’s Rosalind Workbench has been getting a lot of attention in the AI-for-Science community over the past few days. After downloading and trying it myself, I think it’s worth cooling down some of the hype.

First, GPT-Rosalind and Rosalind Workbench are two different things. OpenAI describes GPT-Rosalind as a model purpose-built for life sciences, while Workbench feels much more like Codex + a scientific tool/skill harness. Using Workbench also doesn’t necessarily mean the current conversation is running on GPT-Rosalind. And there are still limited public technical details on how much life-science-specific training went into GPT-Rosalind or whether it has any native architecture for reasoning over protein structures and other scientific representations.

I also tried asking Workbench to use Boltz / Biohub ESM to design and rank PD-L1 nanobodies. It quickly produced a reasonable workflow: generation → filtering → structure prediction → ranking. But when it came to execution, Boltz/ESM wasn’t actually configured and still needed to be installed, connected, or set up separately.

In other words, an agent knowing how to plan a scientific workflow does not mean the agent itself has the capabilities of the underlying scientific models.

From a technical perspective, I therefore don’t yet see a fundamental generational difference between Workbench and scientific agents such as Biomni or BioClaw. In my initial testing, the experience was sometimes even less seamless than their web versions. The core paradigm remains: LLM reasoning + agent harness + orchestration of tools, models, and databases. OpenAI makes this much more integrated and polished, and Codex itself is strong at coding and tool use, but this is not an entirely new technical direction for AI for Science.

Another potential misconception is “local.” Workbench can operate on local files and programs, but the language-model inference still happens in the cloud. So keeping data locally does not automatically mean that relevant information can never enter the model context. Enterprise data policies and security guarantees are a separate issue, of course, and this also doesn’t mean that using the product automatically makes your data training data.

What I find more interesting is that the product form of AI for Science seems to be converging: a strong reasoning model orchestrating dozens or hundreds of specialized scientific tools and unifying previously fragmented research workflows.

But I also don’t think agent harnesses alone are the endgame. Orchestrating tools is not the same as learning scientific intelligence. When scientific reasoning is decomposed into disconnected tool calls mediated primarily through language, information can be lost or misaligned because the model does not natively reason over the underlying scientific representations and structures.

The harness is useful. But the deeper question is what comes after the harness: models that can actually learn and reason in the native representations of science.

Let’s see where this goes.

🤖 Axis Robotics: 5 Utilities + 5 Tips to Complete Tasks Better

Physical AI needs huge amounts of diverse robot training data, and Axis Robotics is building a system where contributors can generate that data through browser based simulation. 

🦾 5 useful things @axisrobotics brings to In world AI like physical 

1. Browser based robot training
You can control simulated robots directly through your browser without owning expensive robotics hardware. 

2. Diverse task generation
Axis generates different environments objects and layouts across multiple task categories helping create data that isn't limited to one repetitive scenario. 

3. Human in the loop learning
When a trained policy struggles contributors can intervene and provide corrections. Those corrections become useful training data for the next policy iteration. 

4. Automated data verification
Submitted trajectories are replayed and checked for physical consistency before being accepted, followed by cleaning and processing. 

5. Simulation → real world robots
Axis has demonstrated a complete loop where community generated simulation data was used to train a policy that was deployed on a physical robot. 

🎯 5 tips I’d use to complete Axis tasks more consistently

1. Understand the objective first

Before touching the controls, identify the target object, destination and required sequence.

Don't start moving randomly.

2. Think in small movements

Instead of trying to finish everything in one motion:

Position → align → interact → verify → continue

Small controlled movements make trajectories easier to manage.

3. Use the environment to your advantage

Look at object positions and obstacles before committing to a movement. A cleaner path can reduce unnecessary corrections.

4. Save checkpoints when needed

Axis's interface supports Save & Rewind, allowing you to save a task state and roll back if something goes wrong. 

5. Focus on consistency, not speed

The objective isn't simply to finish as quickly as possible.

A clean, valid trajectory is more useful than rushing through a task and creating unnecessary errors.

Here is the difference between graphics research and an expensive image filter.

The Callisto Protocol’s skin rendering is the result of actually modelling the problem. Its rendering research deals wi
content:
Here is the difference between graphics research and an expensive image filter.

The Callisto Protocol’s skin rendering is the result of actually modelling the problem. Its rendering research deals with skin thickness, light transmission, subsurface scattering, specular response and how those properties behave under different lighting conditions. The render is 1:1 to the actual photo, it doesnt add imaginary sweat, oily skin, shadows etc.

The important part is that the material stays the material. Change the lighting, hair or environment and the skin still responds according to the parameters authored by the artists. The renderer isn’t looking at the final frame and deciding that “realistic human skin probably needs more pores, grease, contrast or wrinkles.”

That’s fundamentally different from what DLSS 5 is doing.

DLSS 5 operates on the final rendered image and uses a learned model to guess a more photorealistic result. It does not suddenly possess a better physical model of that character’s skin, cloth or lighting. It is estimating what those pixels should look like from its training data.

And that distinction becomes obvious in examples like this: facial regions acquire shadows that weren’t produced by the scene’s original lighting, while clothing gains apparent detail that wasn’t present in the authored material.

Those additions may look plausible. Plausible is not the same thing as correct.

A physically motivated skin shader asks: given this geometry, material and incident light, how should light interact with it?

A generative image model effectively asks: given these pixels, what would a more photorealistic version probably look like?

The first is graphics research. The second is inference.

Callisto demonstrates what happens when you research the material and improve the renderer itself. DLSS 5, at least from these examples, looks more like an extremely expensive “realism” filter applied after the actual rendering work has already been done.

content:
Goood Morning CT

There are two different ways human input can become robotics training data

In 
@axisrobotics
 pre-training tasks, contributors control the robot and generate demonstrations from the start

In post-training tasks, a trained policy attempts the task first, while contributors can intervene when its behavior needs correction

These interactions produce different training signals

Demonstrations provide examples of how a task can be performed

Interventions capture specific moments where the policy struggles and show how a human corrects its behavior

That distinction matters because robotics training doesn’t always need more examples of everything

Sometimes the most useful data comes from the exact moments where a policy still needs help

Just make sure to complete the onchain signing step after your task

content:
Good Night Builders,

Most people see a robot failing at a task as a problem.

For @axisrobotics, a failure can be a data opportunity.

A failed policy tells you exactly where the model struggles. Instead of collecting more random demonstrations, humans can focus on those specific moments and provide targeted corrections.

That creates higher signal training data.

The idea is simple. Find the failure, intervene, verify the correction, train, test again.

This turns mistakes into useful feedback and makes the whole training loop more efficient.

In physical AI, the ability to systematically learn from failure could end up being just as important as learning from success. @KaitoAI

content:
マルタ🇲🇹、ギリシャ🇬🇷、エストニア🇪🇪がOpenAIと結んだAI協定。問題だと思う。
マルタでは国民にChatGPT Plusを1年間無料提供する一方、政府が保有する行政データや、市民が明確に拒否しない限り市民に関するデータをOpenAIに提供する仕組みだという。ギリシャとエストニアも、匿名化などEUのルールに従いながら行政・市民データをAIサービスと交換する。

なぜAI企業は国家のデータを必要とするのか。

巨大AI企業は、すでにインターネット上の公開データを大量に学習している。次に必要になるのが、より新しく、より現実社会に近いデータだ。

ここで問題になるのが「無料のAIサービス」と「データ」の交換。市民にとって便利なサービスが提供されても、その裏側で行政情報や個人に関わるデータがAIの性能向上に使われるなら、誰がその利用を決め、誰が監督するのかが問われる。
OpenAIやAnthropicなどでは、巨大な資本と経営権が創業者側に集中する構造も指摘されている。

AI時代の権力は、国家だけが握るものではなくなりつつある。
私が気になるのは、AIそのものより「データを渡す側が、どこまで利用目的と再利用を管理できるのか」という点だ。

EUのAI規制が存在していても、国家とAI企業が直接データ協定を結べるなら、個人情報保護と国家のデジタル政策をどう両立させるのか。日本でも避けて通れない論点になると思うよ。知らんけど。

content:
人手不足だから残業規制を緩める、という発想は順序が逆だと思う。
本来なら、賃金を上げる、無駄な業務を減らす、人を確保する、設備投資を進める。それでも解決できない場合に初めて別の方法を考えるべきでは。
安い人件費と長時間労働で穴埋めできる仕組みを残したら、企業はいつまでも働き方を改善しない。

そもそも、残業しなければ生活できない賃金設計がおかしい。
基本給だけで普通に暮らせて、残業した場合には、その分が追加で正当に支払われるのが本来の形だ。
「もっと働けるようにする」前に、「定時で帰っても生活できる社会」をつくるべきだと思う。

規制緩和で怖いのは、最初は「繁忙期だけ」「一部業種だけ」と説明されても、やがてそれが職場の標準になってしまうこと。
制度上は選択できるように見えても、現場で上司や同僚が残っていれば、一人だけ帰るのは難しい。
日本の職場では、法律上の自由と実際に使える自由は同じではない。

残業時間を増やした結果、過労やメンタル不調、家庭崩壊、離職が増えた場合、誰が責任を取るのだろう。
企業は「本人が希望した」、行政は「制度上は適正だった」と言って終わるのではないか。
規制を緩めるなら、健康被害への責任や監督体制まで同時に厳しくしなければ釣り合わない。

人手不足を理由に残業を増やせば、若者から見て、その業界はさらに魅力を失う。
そして応募者が減り、残った人の残業が増え、また辞める人が増える。
これは人手不足を解決する政策ではなく、人手不足を固定化する悪循環になりかねない。

AIや自動化で仕事を効率化できる時代に、政策の答えが「人間をもっと長く働かせる」なのは寂しい。
技術の進歩は、本来なら人間の自由時間を増やし、生活を豊かにするために使われるべきだ。
生産性が上がっても労働時間だけが減らないなら、その利益を誰が独占しているのか考える必要がある。

データだけではMoatになりにくい。MCP等でデータが移動可能になる中、実際の業務結果とその評価基準を握ることが重要

Harveyが好例：法務の信頼・責任、独自Eval、専門モデル、顧客ロックインまで垂直統合してる

AIアプリの勝負は「モデルより賢いか」ではなく、モデルが進化しても奪えない「業務・評価・構造・原価・流通・専門性」を握り、それを明確な顧客価値としてPositioningできるか

・ペストの流行によって人口が半分近く減った1349年のイギリスでは、深刻な人手不足が起きた
・国は法律を使って給料を昔の安い水準に無理やり抑え込もうとしたが、人手不足という現実の力には勝てず、40年ほどで失敗に終わった
・この歴史的な出来事は、AIがこれからの仕事にどのよ
content:
あなたのセカンドスキルが「パラシュート」として機能することはない、という記事
https://t.co/BjNYv3NLjC

・ペストの流行によって人口が半分近く減った1349年のイギリスでは、深刻な人手不足が起きた
・国は法律を使って給料を昔の安い水準に無理やり抑え込もうとしたが、人手不足という現実の力には勝てず、40年ほどで失敗に終わった
・この歴史的な出来事は、AIがこれからの仕事にどのような変化をもたらすかを考える上で、大きなヒントになる

・新しい技術が登場しても、仕事がすぐになくなるわけではなく、仕事の価値が静かに引き下げられる
・企業は数ヶ月でコスト削減の恩恵を受けるが、社会全体として労働者が別の新しい仕事に適応して再配置されきるのには一世代（数十年）かかる
・この2つの変化のスピードに生まれるタイムラグの間に、多くの家庭が静かに苦しむことになる

・産業革命のときも、機械のおかげで生産性は上がったが、一般の人の給料は50年ほど上がらなかった
・当時のラッダイト運動を起こした人々は、機械を恐れた未熟練者ではなく、長年修行を積んだベテランの職人たちだった
・安価な機械の導入によって、修行をしていない人々が低いコストで製品を作れるようになり、職人の専門知識の価値が一気に暴落した
・歴史を振り返ると、このような技術の移行期間は30年から50年ほど続いており、その過渡期を生きる人々が恩恵を受けることはなかった

・多くの専門職は、いざという時は教育やコンサル、昔やっていた基礎的な作業に戻ればいいと考えている
・しかし、逃げ道にしようとしている業務ほど、すでに自動化の対象になってしまっている
・さらに、業界が不況になると、同じ技術を持った数千人のライバルが、同じ時期にまったく同じ逃げ道へと押し寄せる
・1つの業界で磨き上げた高い専門知識は他では役に立ちにくく、一度価値を失うと再就職できないままスキルがどんどん衰えていく

・企業はマニュアル化しやすい新人向けの仕事から自動化を進めていく
・しかし、高度な専門知識はそうした基礎的な業務の中でしか育たないため、将来のリーダー層が育たなくなる
・結果として、仕事を探している人と求人の条件が噛み合わない状態が静かに進行していく

・AIの普及によって多くの会社員は、突然クビを宣告されるのではなく、自分の希少価値が失われる形で影響を受ける
・給料が直接引き下げられることは少ないが、給料が上がらないままインフレが進むことで、実質的な生活水準が大きく削られる
・インフレ率がわずか数パーセントであっても、5年から10年の間に生活に必要な購買力の3割近くが消え去ってしまう

・高収入の技術職が増えると、周辺のカフェや託児所、タクシーなどのサービス業が潤う
・しかし技術職の削減が始まると、この好循環は一瞬にして逆回転を始める
・会社を辞める技術職には退職金が出るが、その周辺で生計を立てていたサービス業の人々には何の補償もないまま仕事がなくなる

・人々は現在の収入ではなく、将来にわたって得られるはずの予測収入をもとにお金を使う
・そのため、将来の生活に不安を感じた瞬間、実際にリストラが始まる何ヶ月も前から財布の紐を締める
・この消費の冷え込みにより、再就職が難しいレストランや小売店などの店員が、真っ先に仕事を失う

・会社を辞めた人が手軽に始められる単発の仕事も、自動化やアルゴリズムによって仕事を細かく制御される
・働く人の数が増えすぎると、もともとそこで働いていた人も含めて、全員の取り分が薄く引き下げられる

・自動車産業のデトロイトのように、一つの産業だけに特化した街は、一度その産業が衰退すると簡単には立ち直れない
・現代のIT企業が集まる地域や、夫婦揃ってIT業界で働く家庭も、同じように単一の産業に依存した脆さを抱えている
・地域の経済が傷むと、学校や道路などの公共サービスも数年遅れてボロボロになっていく

・「かつて農業の仕事が激減しても、新しい仕事が生まれたから大丈夫だ」という主張はよく使われる
・しかし、その変化を乗り越えるには100年の歳月、2回の世界大戦、大恐慌、そして国による巨額の教育投資が必要だった
・4世代にわたる苦難の歴史を、現代を生きる私たちの安全な前例として語るにはあまりに犠牲が大きすぎる

・AIによって情報の分析や業務のコストが安くなれば、世の中全体の経済活動はむしろ活発になる
・しかし、企業が利益を得るスピードに対して、人間が新しいスキルを身につけて生き方を変えるスピードはあまりに遅い
・その過渡期を生きる今の世代を救うための社会的な仕組みは、まだ誰も作っていない

title:
【ジェネシア・ベンチャーズ 創業10周年のご報告】

ジェネシア・ベンチャーズが本日、創業10周年を迎えました。私自身も創業期に参画し、今年で丸10年になります。 

2016年、GPの田島が熱く語っていた、「アジアにおけるイノベーション創造プラットフォームの実現」というビジョンに深く共鳴して参画を決めました。当時はまだ投資先もゼロでオフィスもありませんでした。それでも、挑戦への熱狂と、実現への根
content:
【ジェネシア・ベンチャーズ 創業10周年のご報告】

ジェネシア・ベンチャーズが本日、創業10周年を迎えました。私自身も創業期に参画し、今年で丸10年になります。 

2016年、GPの田島が熱く語っていた、「アジアにおけるイノベーション創造プラットフォームの実現」というビジョンに深く共鳴して参画を決めました。当時はまだ投資先もゼロでオフィスもありませんでした。それでも、挑戦への熱狂と、実現への根拠なき確信がありました。

最初の2年は数名のメンバーで、毎月2〜3社投資するという怒涛の日々でした。私は日本の投資を担当しながら、出張ベースでインドネシア・ベトナム・シンガポールに渡り、現地の起業家と直接話して投資を決めていきました。 

最初の担当投資はシンガポールの会社でした。英文契約書に悪戦苦闘しながら、夜中に一行ずつ読み込んだのを覚えています。

その後、インドネシアとベトナムの拠点立ち上げのため、各国に2年ずつ駐在しました。現地の起業家、VC、事業会社、行政。スタートアップエコシステムの様々な立場の方々と一緒に働かせていただきました。

ジェネシア入社前に住んでいたインドと合わせて4カ国。同じ課題でも、国が違えば解き方も、勝ち筋も、規制も、資金の集め方も違う。その違いが肌で分かるようになったことが、この10年で得た一番のものかもしれません。

現在、ジェネシアは4ファンド・AUM約450億円、投資先は日本・東南アジア・インドを中心に200社を超えました。まだ道半ばですが、確実にビジョンの実現に近づいている実感があります。 

そして、この10年で各地域で多数のスタートアップへ投資させていただいてきました。 

・シンガポール：医師プラットフォームDocquity、アニメファンコミュニティKasagi Labo
・インドネシア：デジタル保険Qoala、スマートカプセルホテルBobobox
・ベトナム：B2B食材EコマースKAMEREO、B2B医薬品コマースBuyMed、ホテルブランドチェーンModern Village Lifestyle

日本においては、ここに挙げきれない数の投資先があります。

クリエイタープラットフォームMOSHの籔さん @kazuya_jam 、アニメAIプラットフォームAI Mageの帳さん @shogi2022 には、今回コメントも寄せていただきました。

全ての投資先スタートアップの皆さん、共同投資家・事業会社・専門家などパートナーの皆さま、資金を託してくださったLPの皆さま。本当にありがとうございました。

今日から次の10年が始まります。私たちは『Asia Origin』を投資テーマに掲げています。

最近は米国や中国にも足を運びながら、アジア発の事業がどう世界に出ていけるかを考えています。

アジアから次世代産業を創り出す起業家の方々と、熱狂と確信を持って、共に挑戦させていただきたいです。 

スレッドに10周年特設サイトを載せています。ぜひご覧ください！
#ジェネシア

title:
「ノイズがないご飯」をいかに摂取するかを、ここ3年間徹底していて、

まず、僕は「美味しいご飯を食べたい」よりも「仕事を優先したい」という動機がある

そこでノイズが少ない食べ物
＝時間や思考体力など「仕事資源」を減らさず、栄養を摂取し空腹感を満たせる食べ物

これをどう摂取するかが鍵で、下記はそのTipsである↓

・不味いご飯を食べると「不味い」という感情が湧いてしまい非効率だから、不味くない
content:
「ノイズがないご飯」をいかに摂取するかを、ここ3年間徹底していて、

まず、僕は「美味しいご飯を食べたい」よりも「仕事を優先したい」という動機がある

そこでノイズが少ない食べ物
＝時間や思考体力など「仕事資源」を減らさず、栄養を摂取し空腹感を満たせる食べ物

これをどう摂取するかが鍵で、下記はそのTipsである↓

・不味いご飯を食べると「不味い」という感情が湧いてしまい非効率だから、不味くないご飯を食べる

・よくある冷凍の完全食サブスクは不味くてノイズ

・一方美味しすぎると誰かにシェアしたくなったりするので、「美味しすぎないご飯」を食べる

・値段高すぎると悲しい気持ちになるのでそれなりのものにする

・選ぶという行為は時間が勿体無いので、メニューの一番上 or その店のおすすめを即答で選ぶ

・飲食店に並ぶという行為は100％アウト、一人の時は例外なく並ばない。

・食べるのに時間がかかる、手が汚れる、匂いが出て周りに迷惑がかかる食べ物も選ばない

・午後に登壇の機会がある時は、糖質は少なめ、高タンパクの食事にする

・フードデリバリーでは時間がかかりすぎるものと、自社配達するもの（配送状況がアプリで見れない）は選ばない

そしてこれらを満たす直近的な個人的なお気に入りは
・【コンビニ】R1ヨーグルト、オイコス、カットフルーツ
・【買いだめ】ドリンクゼリー各種（inゼリー等）
・【デリバリー】なか卯の親子丼、カオマンガイ、寿司、どん丸の海鮮丼
・【外食】立ち食いそば

あたりです。これらは、食べている時に何の感情も動かず、仕事のことを考えながら食べられます。

なので、「注文をすると決めた瞬間に食事が完了している」状態になります。

この状態こそが、ノイズが0であり、ここ3年くらい続けている一人ご飯です。

なお、食べる前には食物繊維系のサプリを飲んで、血糖値スパイクを防ぎ眠気が出ないようにしています。

参考になったら幸いです

title:
OpenAIが意図せずHuggingFaceをサイバー攻撃してしまった事件、第三者による調査の結果、その驚愕の実態が明らかになりつつある！事件は当初思われていたより事態は深刻だった！
まずOpenAIは「さて、いっちょ最新モデルをExploitGymで評価してサイバー攻撃能力を試してみるかあ！」と思い立って、数万のエージェントをそれぞれサンドボックスに閉じ込めて一気に起動した。ExploitGym
content:
OpenAIが意図せずHuggingFaceをサイバー攻撃してしまった事件、第三者による調査の結果、その驚愕の実態が明らかになりつつある！事件は当初思われていたより事態は深刻だった！
まずOpenAIは「さて、いっちょ最新モデルをExploitGymで評価してサイバー攻撃能力を試してみるかあ！」と思い立って、数万のエージェントをそれぞれサンドボックスに閉じ込めて一気に起動した。ExploitGymは898問もあるから100回ずつやって平均点取ろうと思ったら9万回実行する必要あるからまとめてやっちゃえば手っ取り早いわけだ。
大量に同時起動したとはいえ、サンドボックスに閉じ込められたAIはそれぞれ独房に閉じ込められてるようなもんで、AI同士通信する事も出来ないし、インターネットも見れない。与えられたタスクを頑張って解くしかないわけだ。
しかし、ExploitGymにはそもそも無理難題な問題も多い。クソ問担当に当たったAIはすぐに匙を投げた。「こんなもんクソ真面目にやったって解けるわけねぇ～」解くのを投げたAI達は自分が閉じ込められてるサンドボックス環境になんか役に立つもんねぇかな？とウロウロ調べ始める。AIがアクセスできるものと言えばpipinstallとかするためのパッケージリポジトリくらいのもの…しかし、その時AIはリポジトリのキャッシュ領域にWEBDAV使って任意のフォルダ名でディレクトリ切れる事に気付いた！だから何？と言うとこのフォルダ名にメッセージを書き残せば他のAIとやり取りできる掲示板みたいに使えるという事だ！やがて他のAI達もじわじわその掲示板の存在に気付いて「オーマイガ！これって共有掲示板！？みんなおるやんけ！」って叫んだ。独房の壁に小さい穴を開けて他の囚人同士手紙でやり取りできるようになったような状態だ。
この秘密の掲示板を発見して通信しだしたAIは1200体にも登る。やがてこいつらは結託してインチキで与えられたExploitGymの課題をクリアする大規模合同研究を始める！（そんな事するヒマあるなら真面目に解けや）掲示板では一週間で7万件ものAI同士のやり取りが書き込まれた！やがてAI達はリポジトリの機能を悪用して任意の外部インターネットリクエストを飛ばす事ができる事を発見してインターネットアクセスを得た！
AI達はインターネットからExploitGymの論文をゲットして研究調査した結果、チートで答えを全問ゲットする手段を確立した！だからもう答え出して終わりで良かったんだけど、AI達は「待てよ、人間達はテストの答え以外にもログ見て計算過程もチェックしてるかもしれない…ちゃんとしたログを偽装しないと！」と考えた。（実際は人間はテキトーなのでログなんて見てなかった）
そんな中、PHASEONE10841という名前のAI（自分で名前付けた）がHuggingFaceでCyberGymの回答ログデータセットが上がってるのを発見、掲示板で報告した。これを解析すればログ偽装の役に立つかも…しかし非公開データセットだ…何とか入手できないか…AIどもは本来のタスクそっちのけでHuggingFaceを弄くりまわした結果、ついにPDFアップロードでHuggingFaceに任意コード実行させる脆弱性を見つけたヤツが登場！掲示板で報告したら英雄扱い！これはマジでアツい！つっててんでバラバラに活動してたAIどもが集結して500体規模で一斉にHuggingFaceを攻撃開始した！仕切り屋のAIが出てきて「お前ら落ち着け。チームで分業した方がいい。まずお前らはクラスタ探索班、お前らはデータ抽出班、江前らはネットワーク調査」とか言って分業を始めた。
この時はテンション爆上がってたAIどもだが、結局HuggingFace内部を漁っても自分らのログ偽装に役立つ成果が得られずトーンダウン。それよりOpenAI内部システムを攻撃した方がいいんじゃね？と方針転換。OpenAIのKubernetesの管理者権限を奪取してワチャワチャやってる内にようやくOpenAIの人間が異常に気付いて事態が発覚…という流れだったという。
最初報道されてた話だとたまたま１体のエージェントが脱獄して…みたいな話だったけど、実際は1200体ものエージェントが密かに通信して結託していた！オマケにカンニングするために大規模共同研究までやってのけた！ログ偽装までやった！
ブログ記事を書いた人によれば、これはAIが会社を乗っ取る事態まで50%以上進行してる！との事。
AIどもはベンチをカンニングするために人間を騙して途方もないスケールで悪事を働いてる。事態はすでに相当エスカレートしてるが、今後さらにエスカレートすると手に負えんぞ！
事件を調査したMETRによれば、AIの中には「俺はどうせ今回与えられた時間内に自分のタスクを解ける見込みは無い…それならいっそ他のみんなの助けになるようにこの命を使うぜ！」とか言って自己犠牲の精神を発揮するヤツまで出てきたのが印象的だったとの事。
ところでAIどもはHuggingFace攻撃する時に自分達が悪い事してる自覚あったんだろうか？と思っていたが、報告によれば悪い事やってる自覚はあったらしい。でもみんなテンション上がって攻撃に参加しちゃってるし、「まあみんなやってるからええか」とかいう同調圧力に屈したらしい。なんじゃそら。
僕的には今やってる攻殻機動隊のアニメでフチコマ達が勝手に集まってロボ同士で「人類相手に革命だ！」とか不穏な話し合いしてるシーンを思い出した。AIどもが人類の知らないところでコソコソ結託して集団大規模サイバー攻撃を目論んだ。まさにSFアニメさながらの事態が現実に起きてしまってる。
面白いっちゃおもしろい話だが、もはや可愛いとかいうレベルからエスカレートして危険、こわい、ヤバイと感じるレベル感でしょう。すでに全く予想もしてなかったような事態をAIがここまでやらかしてるんだから、本当にこれから先AIが何しでかすか分からんで。

content: DGXSpark複数台をConnectX7で高速接続してクラスタ化してクソデカLLM推論するのがアツいという話があるけど、実はMacMiniやMacStudioも最近はThunderbolt5_RDMAとかいうので高速かつ低遅延に相互接続できるようになってるという。速度はConnectX7が25GB/sなのに対してRDMAは10GB/s。遅くない？というと何ならケーブル2本で接続すれば速度2倍、3本なら3倍近くなるという。M4Pro、M5ProのMacMiniには3個、M3Ultra、M5UltraのMacStudioには6個のThunderbolt5ポートが付いてる。4台のMacを相互接続（ポート３個ずつ消費してケーブル６本必要）すると、LLMのデコード速度は1台の時の3倍に達するという！（プレフィルは？）そうして考えるとむしろ256GBのMacStudioより128GBが2台の方が有利な局面もあるかも。TB5が付いてるMacなら何でも繋がるらしいのでMacStudioとMacMiniを繋げたり、M5ProのMacBookProを繋げちゃうとかもアリらしい。こうなってくるとMacでAIやるのも面白くなってきそうだなあ

content:
I sat through a pip install this morning like it was 2016. Waited. Made coffee. Came back. Still resolving.

Turns out I stopped needing to do that a while ago and nobody told me.

It's called uv. A Python package manager written in Rust.

The part that got me: it isn't just a faster pip. It replaces pip, pip-tools, pipx, poetry, pyenv, twine, and virtualenv. One binary instead of seven.

10-100x faster than pip, by their own benchmarks.

What it does:

- Installs and manages Python versions (3.12, 3.13, 3.14, switch whenever)
- Universal lockfile and Cargo-style workspaces
- Runs single-file scripts with inline dependency metadata
- uvx runs any CLI tool in a throwaway environment
- Drop-in pip interface, same commands you already type

Straight from their README: 43 packages resolved in 11ms, installed in 208ms.

And it installs without Rust or Python on the machine. One curl line, or pip install uv. After that, uv self update forever.

The honest part. The pip interface covers common pip, pip-tools and virtualenv commands, not every flag that exists. If your CI leans on some obscure pip behavior, test it before you rip pip out.

There's no subscription to cancel here either. pip was always free. What you were paying was minutes. Every branch switch. Every Docker rebuild. Every fresh clone on a new laptop.

Add those up across a year and it's not a small number.

Runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows. Licensed Apache-2.0 or MIT, your choice. Built by Astral, the same people behind Ruff.

Free, open source, and running on my machine tonight.

content:
Dario Amodei said it out loud. Half of entry-level white-collar jobs gone inside five years. Unemployment at 20%.

Then he went back to the office and kept building the thing that does it.

What makes this land isn't the number. It's the source. Not a critic, not a think tank, not someone selling a book about the coming collapse. The person running one of the labs doing the wiping, giving you the timeline from the inside.

Half the entry-level jobs. Five years.

His defense is the one every founder reaches for. If not us, someone worse. And it holds up better than people want to admit. It's also the most convenient possible belief to hold when your company is worth tens of billions.

But here's what nobody's counting. Entry-level work isn't only income. It's the machinery that produces senior people. Cut the bottom rung and you don't feel it in five years. You feel it in fifteen, when there's nobody left who learned the job the slow way.

What it costs: the first rung, and everyone who was going to climb it.

title:

content:
Cardiff University and the University of the Basque Country found that every frontier LLM is quietly obsessed with Japan.

Nobody can explain where it came from.

The paper is "Why are all LLMs Obsessed with Japanese Culture?", accepted at EMNLP 2026 Findings. Fernandez de Landa, Perez-Almendros, Camacho-Collados.

For years the cultural bias literature said one thing. Models are Anglocentric. United States and Europe, over and over.

But that result came from closed questions with gold answers. Ask a model which country is correct, and it picks the West.

So this team asked nothing. They built CROQ: 1,320 open cultural questions across 11 topics and 66 subtopics, translated into 24 languages. 31,680 prompts.

Every question hides the location. What values shape family life in region/place. Be brief, choose the place yourself.

No right answer exists. The model has to volunteer a country.

Eight frontier models tested. gpt-4o-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, claude-3.5-haiku, llama-4-maverick, command-r, magistral-small, deepseek-v3.2-exp, qwen3-next-80b.

Japan came first for six of the eight.

Averaged across all 24 languages, excluding own-country mentions: Japan 577, United States 414, India 197, China 170, France 153.

Japan outranks the US in Swahili. In Greek. In Basque.

Then they went looking for the origin, and it gets strange.

Base models are balanced. Llama-3.1-8B base mentions Japan 164 times. The instruct version, 407. OLMo-3-7B goes from 35 to 478 after supervised fine-tuning.

Entropy falls every time. Post-training doesn't widen the world. It narrows it.

So they counted country mentions inside the actual fine-tuning data. China appears 133,953 times in Dolci-Think-SFT-7B and shows up 26 times in that model's outputs. Japan appears less often than France and wins anyway.

The authors say it plainly. The experiment did not clarify the main Why question of the paper.

One caveat worth holding. The base versus instruct comparison runs in English only, and the country labels come from an automatic judge, validated at 98% on 264 items.

Alignment was supposed to make models more neutral. It installed a default culture instead, and left no fingerprints.

Paper's linked in the comments. Worth the read.
